lead: Real circuits mix series branches and parallel branches. Elements in series share one current; elements in parallel share one voltage. Reduction folds the whole network into a single resistance, finds the source current from Ohm's law, then unfolds step by step with the voltage and current divider rules to reach any branch quantity. An electrician tracing a faulty branch of house wiring, or an engineer reading a sensor bridge, uses exactly this. Some syllabi call the topic network reduction techniques.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for element values and Chapter 1.3 for Ohm's law and the KVL and KCL proofs behind both divider rules.

sections.h3: Series and parallel: one current, one voltage

blocks.text: Two elements are in series when the same current must pass through both — they sit on one path with no junction between them. They are in parallel when both connect across the same two nodes, so both see the same voltage.

blocks.where: R_s is the total series resistance in ohms (Ω); R1 … Rn are the individual resistances in ohms. The same current I = V/R_s flows through every element, and the drops add to V by KVL.
R_p is the equivalent parallel resistance in ohms; each R is a branch resistance in ohms. For exactly two resistors, R_p = R1R2/(R1+R2), the product over the sum.

blocks.text: Conductance G = 1/R is measured in siemens (S); 1 S = 1 A/V. It adds directly: G_p = G1 + G2, in siemens. That is why adding a branch always lowers the equivalent resistance and raises the source current.

items: R_p is always smaller than the smallest branch resistance.
n equal resistors R in parallel give R/n; two equal resistors give R/2.
Convert kΩ to Ω before combining — never add 4 Ω to 12 kΩ.

sections.h3: Voltage divider and current divider rules

blocks.text: Two series resistors across a source V carry the same current I = V/(R1+R2). Ohm's law on R1 gives the voltage divider.

blocks.where: V1 is the voltage across R1 in volts; V is the source voltage in volts; R1 and R2 are in ohms. The bigger resistor takes the bigger share.

blocks.text: Two parallel resistors carrying a total current I share it in inverse proportion to resistance. The current divider puts the other resistance on top.

blocks.where: I1 is the current through R1 in amperes; I is the total current entering the pair in amperes; R1 and R2 are in ohms. The smaller resistor carries the larger current.

blocks.text: For three or more branches, first find R_p, then I_k = I × R_p/R_k, where R_k is the branch whose current you want. The voltage across the bank is I R_p, and each branch current is that voltage divided by its own resistance.

Inductors follow resistors: series L = L1 + L2 + …, parallel 1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2 + …. Capacitors run the other way: series 1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + …, parallel C = C1 + C2 + …. A capacitive divider splits voltage inversely with capacitance.

sections.h3: Ladder networks, open branches and short branches

blocks.text: A ladder network alternates series arms and shunt arms. Work from the end farthest from the source toward it.

items: Circle each parallel group and mark its two nodes.
Combine the group farthest from the source into one resistance.
Add that to the series arm feeding it.
Repeat until one resistance R_total remains; the source current is V/R_total.
Unfold outward: current divider at each parallel node, voltage divider along each series arm.

blocks.text: An open branch has infinite resistance. Delete it and recompute the network: its own current becomes zero, and the currents and voltages elsewhere usually change. A branch connected directly across an ideal source is the exception — removing it leaves the other branch values unchanged. A short branch has zero resistance. Placed across a parallel group it forces that group's equivalent resistance to zero and the group voltage to zero, so every element in parallel with the short is bypassed — no current through it, no voltage across it. Elements elsewhere, including the series arms feeding the shorted section, still carry current, and their current rises.

A loaded divider is not the unloaded one. Connect a load R_L across R2 and R_L sits in parallel with R2. The section resistance falls, so the output voltage falls. Reduce R2 ∥ R_L first, then apply the divider rule; the unloaded value is only an upper bound.

figure.caption: The parallel pair 12 Ω ∥ 6 Ω becomes 4 Ω, which adds to 4 Ω and 2 Ω to give 10 Ω, so the source current is 24/10 = 2.4 A.

spec.title: Reducing a network step by step
spec.aria: A four-step reduction: the parallel pair becomes 4 Ω, the series total becomes 10 Ω, and the source current becomes 2.4 A.

examples.question: A 24 V DC source supplies R1 = 4 Ω in series with a parallel pair R2 = 12 Ω and R3 = 6 Ω, then R4 = 2 Ω back to the source. Find (a) the total resistance, (b) the source current, (c) the voltage across the parallel pair, and (d) the current in R2 and in R3. Verify KCL at the parallel node.
steps: Voltage across the pair: the 2.4 A flows through the 4 Ω equivalent, V23 = 2.4 × 4 = 9.6 V. Check by divider: V23 = 24 × 4/10 = 9.6 V.
Current in R2: I2 = 9.6/12 = 0.8 A. Current in R3: I3 = 9.6/6 = 1.6 A.
KCL: 0.8 + 1.6 = 2.4 A, equal to the source current.
examples.answer: R_total = 10 Ω, source current = 2.4 A, pair voltage = 9.6 V, I_R2 = 0.8 A and I_R3 = 1.6 A.
examples.check:
V = 24.0
R1, R2, R3, R4 = 4.0, 12.0, 6.0, 2.0
R23 = R2*R3/(R2+R3)
R_total = R1 + R23 + R4
I = V/R_total
V23 = I*R23
I2 = V23/R2
I3 = V23/R3
print(R_total)
print(I)
print(V23)
print(I2)
print(I3)

examples.question: A 10 A current enters a parallel network. Branch 1 is 4 Ω. Branch 2 is 6 Ω in series with 4 Ω. Find the current in each branch.
steps: Current divider check: I1 = 10 × 10/14 = 7.14 A; I2 = 10 × 4/14 = 2.86 A. Sum = 10 A.
examples.answer: I1 = 7.14 A in the 4 Ω branch, I2 = 2.86 A in the 10 Ω branch.
examples.check:
I = 10.0
R1 = 4.0
R2 = 6.0 + 4.0
Rp = R1*R2/(R1+R2)
V = I*Rp
I1 = V/R1
I2 = V/R2
print(R2)
print(Rp)
print(I1)
print(I2)

traps: Current divider upside down: I1 = I × R2/(R1+R2), not I × R1/(R1+R2). The resistance whose current you want sits at the bottom; the other one is on top.
Forgetting to invert the reciprocal: 1/R_p = 1/4 + 1/12 gives 1/3, so R_p = 3 Ω, not 1/3 Ω.
Capacitors follow the opposite pattern to resistors: series adds reciprocals, parallel adds directly. Memorising only the resistor pattern fails on capacitors.
Using the unloaded voltage divider when a load is connected. The load sits in parallel with R2 and pulls the output down; include it before dividing.
Mixing units: 4 Ω and 12 kΩ cannot be combined until both are in the same unit. A factor-of-1000 slip is the usual cause of a wrong source current.

quiz.q: Write the formula for two resistors in parallel and name each symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: R_p = R1R2/(R1+R2); R_p is the equivalent resistance in Ω, R1 and R2 are the branch resistances in Ω.

quiz.q: How do inductors in series combine? How do capacitors in parallel combine?
quiz.a: Inductors in series add like resistors: L = L1 + L2. Capacitors in parallel add directly: C = C1 + C2.

quiz.q: Why is the equivalent resistance of a parallel group always smaller than its smallest branch?
quiz.a: Each extra branch gives current another conducting path. Conductance adds: G_p = G1 + G2 + …, so R_p = 1/G_p falls. If only the smallest branch were present, the group resistance would equal that smallest branch. Every extra branch adds conductance, so the full group is smaller than the smallest branch.

quiz.q: Two resistors 6 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel and carry a total current of 3 A. Find the current in each.
A 12 V source feeds 2 Ω in series with the parallel pair 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Find total resistance, source current and the voltage across the pair.
R1 = 10 Ω and R2 = 10 Ω are across a 20 V source. A 10 Ω load is then connected across R2. Find the new output voltage and explain the change.
quiz.a: R2 ∥ 10 = 5 Ω; R_total = 10 + 5 = 15 Ω; I = 20/15 = 1.333 A; V_out = 1.333 × 5 = 6.67 V. The load lowers the resistance of the R2 section, so more of the 20 V drops across R1 and the output falls from its unloaded 10 V.

quiz.q: A 10 A current enters a parallel network. Branch 1 is 4 Ω; branch 2 is 6 Ω in series with 4 Ω. Find each branch current.
quiz.a: Branch 2 = 10 Ω; R_p = 4 × 10/14 = 2.857 Ω; V = 28.57 V; I1 = 28.57/4 = 7.14 A; I2 = 28.57/10 = 2.86 A. Sum = 10 A. The series element inside branch 2 must be added before applying the current divider.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every circuit simulator combines series and parallel elements before it builds its matrix — reduction is step zero of SPICE-class tools. PCB designers use the same divider arithmetic to set feedback nodes in voltage regulators. Battery packs are wired series-parallel to fix both voltage and capacity. Search next for 'ladder network reduction', 'loaded voltage divider' and 'equivalent resistance'. Then try a bridge: it is neither series nor parallel, which is why it needs Chapter 1.5.
